.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 220 PM EDT Wednesday...

1. Showers are expected to continue this afternoon and evening 
before drier and seasonable weather returns as we head into the 
weekend.

2. Showers and thunderstorm chances increase by the end of the 
weekend with unsettled weather continuing into early next week. 
Temperatures will be relatively seasonable through the extended 
period.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 220 PM EDT Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A dying cold front is approaching northern New York and 
Vermont from Canada this afternoon, producing some showers out ahead 
of it. The forcing will decrease as it moves east through northern 
New York, but enough instability is out there to allow the showers 
to continue into Vermont. A couple embedded thunderstorms are 
possible as well. While sufficient deep layer shear will be in place 
for potentially strong storms, low instability, some dry air aloft, 
a lack of well-defined surface boundary, and pre-existing 
clouds/showers will be working against it. Therefore, an isolated 
strong to severe storm is not likely this afternoon, but cannot be 
completely ruled out. Any storms will fall apart as they try to push 
southeast this evening and southern areas should remain mostly dry. 
Chances of lingering showers overnight are around 10-40%, mainly 
near the international border. High pressure will build down from 
Canada to end the week and start the weekend, bringing cooler 
temperatures and lower humidity. Lows tonight will be seasonable in 
the 50s, then cooling late week into the 40s and 50s. Highs through 
Saturday will be seasonable, with temperatures rising into the 70s 
and low 80s each afternoon. Next chance of precipitation arrives 
later Saturday afternoon onward.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A quasi-double barrel pattern will develop by late 
Saturday with competing pieces of energy, one over central-eastern 
Ontario, and a coastal low in southern New England. Models depict a 
deepening trough over the Great Lakes by Saturday with a coastal low 
riding along the coast of southern New England. The deepening of the 
Great Lakes trough will help amplify our flow pattern aloft Saturday 
night into Sunday, likely accelerating the coastal low 
northeastward. A few showers will be possible on the periphery of 
the coastal low Saturday night in southeastern Vermont, though 
majority of Vermont will stay dry Saturday and Saturday night. In 
northern New York, the Great Lakes trough will lead to increasing 
shower chances late Saturday into Saturday night across the St. 
Lawrence Valley and northwestern Adirondacks. Questions linger on 
how much moisture will be sandwiched between the two systems closer 
to Sunday morning, as it pertains to precipitation chances in 
Vermont. Currently there is a 35-50% chance of rain Sunday morning 
for much of Vermont, though these values may increase or decrease 
with how the trough amplification occurs. A more delayed 
amplification could keep the coastal system from racing east with a 
moisture interaction in the area between the system Sunday morning. 
A faster amplification will likely lead to less system interactions 
and perhaps a dry Sunday morning. Regardless, as the Great Lakes 
trough translates east Sunday, everyone will see periods of rain, 
and perhaps some thunderstorms should enough clearing take place to 
allow instability to grow. Temperatures will start off on the warmer 
than average side in the upper 70s to low 80s, though with the 
approach of clouds and showers, temperatures by Sunday will begin a 
gradual decrease back to seasonable levels.

The main piece of energy departs late Sunday, though cyclonic flow 
about a trailing upper low over eastern Ontario will keep some 
shower chances around. Lingering showers will be focused over the 
higher terrain Monday and Tuesday afternoon, mainly diurnally 
driven. Sky cover Monday and Tuesday will favor more clouds then sun 
as a result of the scattered shower chances. Temperatures will 
remain on the seasonable to potentially slightly below seasonable 
levels Monday and Tuesday with highs in the low to mid 70s. 
Temperatures will rebound by mid week with subtle ridging building 
over eastern New England.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z WEDNESDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
Through 18Z Thursday...A slow moving cold front is moving through the
region, weakening as it moves east. The boundary is broken into two
parts. An initial area of isolated light showers and drizzle
currently from eastern Franklin County VT to SLK, and a secondary
area of more moderate scattered showers in the St. Lawrence Valley.
The first round will be unimpactful showers for EFK/BTV/PBG/MPV.
However, the second round could bring brief MVFR vsbys under any
showers, with higher confidence in any reductions at MSS/SLK for the
next hour or two. Confidence wains as this secondary boundary slides
east, though about a 30% chance for any vsbys reductions exists at
BTV/PBG/EFK/MPV. RUT should remain dry through this afternoon. The
front then washes out over the area with lingering low level
moisture for tonight. The question then becomes does this moisture
scour out in the mid levels for fog potential, or does this low
level moisture remain fairly thick with more low level stratus.
Regardless, most sites will likely see some reductions at least to
MVFR cigs and vsby tonight with moisture lingering. Confidence in
fog will increase should a terminal receive a shower close to sunset
or 23-01Z. Models depict some easterly flow at BTV which could draw
some VCFG at the least near sunset. Highest probabilities for fog
(around 40-50%) exist at SLK/MPV, with slightly lower probs (30-40%)
at MSS/EFK. Trends upstream suggest low stratus may initially spread
over the area transitioning to more fog closer to sunrise. Any low
clouds scour out by tomorrow morning with mainly high clouds through
the end of the TAF period. Winds will generally remain west to
southwest today, becoming light and variable overnight into tomorrow
morning.
